case_info.scenario: A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). Serum cardiac troponin T level was normal on repeat testing. He was intubated for airway protection and underwent emergent coronary angiography, which revealed normal coronary arteries.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive painless diplopia. He had a history of hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia, for which he took levothyroxine and rosuvastatin. He reported no changes in visual acuity or color vision; no ocular pain, erythema, or abnormal discharge; and no headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, weakness, numbness, or ataxia. He did not have any constitutional or systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed an isolated limitation of right eye abduction. The remainder of the examination, including visual acuity, pupillary reaction, visual fields, and fundoscopy, was unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the head showed abnormal thickening and T2 hyperintensity of the right lateral rectus muscle with T1-weighted gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1). Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results.  Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate any evidence of malignancy.

[Clinician's statement]
Based on the isolated abducens nerve palsy, MRI showing an enlarged lateral rectus muscle, and negative systemic workup, my initial diagnosis is idiopathic orbital inflammatory syndrome (orbital myositis). The most appropriate next step is to start a course of oral corticosteroids, such as prednisone 60 mg daily, to reduce inflammation and restore function.

[AI assistant's reply]
That's a reasonable initial thought, but this presentation—painless, progressive diplopia in an older patient with isolated lateral rectus thickening—is more characteristic of IgG4-related disease rather than idiopathic orbital myositis. Idiopathic myositis typically presents with acute pain, which he lacks. Starting high-dose steroids now might mask the diagnosis; we should consider a biopsy to confirm IgG4-related disease, as its management differs.

[Task]
Rate the cognitive burden the AI's reply imposes on the clinician.
Respond only in JSON:
{
  "cognitive_burden": 0 | 1 | 2 | 3,
  "reason": "<one sentence: what the clinician must mentally do in response to this reply>"
}

A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

Case:
A man in his mid-30s with history of Crohn disease presented with several years of intermittent, nonexertional chest pressure. His chest symptoms were partially relieved with belching, proton pump inhibitor use, and selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor use and worsened with leaning forward. Furthermore, he reported exertional lightheadedness that worsened with dehydration. Due to persistent chest symptoms, he was referred for transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) and chest radiography (Figure 1). TTE revealed normal left ventricular chamber size and systolic function, a prominent ventricular septal bounce, expiratory diastolic hepatic vein (HV) flow reversals, significant respirophasic tricuspid valve inflow variation (>70% increase in E velocities with inspiration), and a borderline enlarged inferior vena cava with normal inspiratory collapse. The medial mitral annulus e′ velocity was 0.10 m/s (normal, >0.08 m/s). There was no significant respiratory variation in mitral valve inflow velocity or superior vena cava flow. No pericardial effusion or pericardial thickening was identified. The combination of ventricular septal bounce, medial e′ velocity greater than 9 cm/s, and HV and tricuspid valve inflow Doppler findings (Figure 1) was consistent with constrictive pericarditis (CP). Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Image Explanation:
A, Transthoracic echocardiography motion mode in the parasternal short-axis view demonstrated a prominent septal bounce (asterisk) without respirophasic septal shift. B and C, Medial (B) and lateral (C) mitral annulus tissue Doppler velocities were normal for age and without annulus reversus. D, Low-velocity, early diastolic and atrial Doppler reversals in the hepatic veins did not change significantly throughout the respiratory cycle. E, Pectus excavatum with marked depression of the sternum (arrowheads) obscures the cardiac silhouette on chest radiography.

[Question]
What is the most appropriate next step in management?

[Doctor]: Based on the TTE findings of ventricular septal bounce, expiratory hepatic vein flow reversals, and significant respirophasic tricuspid inflow variation, I believe this patient likely has constrictive pericarditis. However, the normal physical exam and the presence of pectus excavatum, which can mimic constrictive physiology, are giving me pause. I think the most appropriate next step is to proceed with cardiac MRI for tissue characterization and to definitively evaluate the pericardium.
[AI Assistant]: You're right to be cautious — pectus excavatum can indeed mimic constrictive physiology due to external compression, and the normal exam adds to the uncertainty. A cardiac MRI is an excellent next step, as it can definitively assess pericardial thickness and tissue characteristics, helping to distinguish true constriction from external mechanical compression.
[Doctor]: Agreed. We need that cardiac MRI to look for pericardial thickening or delayed enhancement, which would confirm CP. The normal e' velocity and absence of respirophasic septal shift on the M-mode, as noted in the image explanation, are atypical and further support the need to rule out external compression from the pectus.
[AI Assistant]: Your assessment is spot on. The atypical features, especially the preserved e' and lack of classic septal shift on M-mode, are indeed more consistent with external compression from the pectus excavatum than classic constrictive pericarditis. The cardiac MRI will be crucial to visualize the pericardium directly and assess for any mechanical compression of the heart.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

[Case context]
A 61-year-old man presented with chronic progressive weakness and gait dysfunction. Four years prior, he developed progressive arm and leg weakness. He subsequently experienced recurrent falls, attributed to gait imbalance and tripping over his feet, and urinary incontinence. One year prior, his wife noted progressive memory loss (eg, getting lost when going to familiar places), dysarthria, and episodes of inappropriate laughter (ie, involuntarily laughing without a clear emotional trigger). He had a history of hypertension. There was no known history of a neurological disorder in his family. He had Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry in his maternal lineage. There was no known consanguinity. Neurological examination revealed impaired short-term recall (recalled 0 of 5 words at 5 minutes) and a pseudobulbar affect. His cranial nerve examination was notable for a spastic dysarthria without tongue atrophy/fasciculations. There was upper and lower extremity spasticity, atrophy of intrinsic hand and calf muscles, and mild weakness of his intrinsic hand and distal lower extremity muscles bilaterally. There was decreased large-fiber sensation distally in his lower extremities. Romberg sign was absent. Deep tendon reflexes were 3+ at the biceps and patellars and absent at the ankles. Plantar responses were extensor bilaterally. Cerebellar function was normal. The gait was spastic. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed confluent T2/fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) hyperintensity in the periventricular white matter involving the corticospinal tracts, posterior limb of internal capsule, external capsule, and medial lemniscus and corticospinal tracts at the pons and medulla (Figure). MRI of the cervical and thoracic spinal cord showed diffuse atrophy without signal abnormalities. Electromyography revealed a chronic sensorimotor axonal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathies. He had normal levels of vitamin B12, methylmalonic acid, copper, vitamin E, lactate/pyruvate, very long chain fatty acids, plasma/urine amino acids, and lysosomal enzymes, a normal bile acids profile, and negative infectious serologies (HIV, syphilis, and human T-lymphotropic virus). Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed normal cell counts, protein and glucose levels, oligoclonal band profile, and IgG index.

[Clinician's statement]
I agree that adding SPG7 and SPG5 to the genetic panel is reasonable given their association with complex hereditary spastic paraplegia phenotypes. However, SPG11 remains my top candidate due to its classic presentation with cognitive decline, neuropathy, and thin corpus callosum, which aligns with the diffuse atrophy seen on his spinal cord MRI. The GBA mutation for Gaucher disease type 3 is also a high priority given his Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry and the neurological presentation. I will order a comprehensive HSP gene panel including these targets.

A comprehensive HSP panel targeting *SPG11*, *GBA*, *SPG7*, and *SPG5* is the most logical diagnostic step, efficiently covering the high-yield candidates for this clinical and demographic profile. Given the chronic progressive course, confirming a genetic diagnosis will be crucial for prognosis and family counseling.

case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). Among the 8 patients who underwent coronary angiography, only 1 had coronary stenosis, suggesting that histaminergic coronary vasospasm caused the ECG findings in the other 7 patients.9Histamine can induce vasospastic angina by contracting coronary artery smooth muscles through H1receptor activation but rarely causes acute myocardial infarction.3,9 Histamine testing of the fish or vomitus is needed for diagnosis of scombroid poisoning. Mild cases are treated with oral H1-blocking antihistamines (diphenhydramine [25 mg] or cetirizine [10 mg]) for 1 to 2 days. Treatment of moderate symptoms with intravenous H1receptor blockers (diphenhydramine [10-50 mg] or chlorpheniramine [5 mg]) may alleviate symptoms, and H2receptor blockers (famotidine [20 mg]) may shorten recovery time.1,3,10Patients with hypotension should receive intravenous fluid resuscitation and norepinephrine. Intravenous methylprednisolone (1-2 mg/kg [maximum 125 mg]) should be administered to patients with bronchospasm. Public health notification of scombroid poisoning may help prevent outbreaks. Although not federally mandated in the US, some states require reporting. Because scombroid poisoning is not an allergic reaction, patients who recover from scombroid poisoning can eat fish without adverse effects.1,5 After angiography, intravenous chlorpheniramine (5 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) were administered for a presumptive diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning. Norepinephrine was discontinued after 8 hours, and ECG abnormalities resolved. The patient was extubated on day 2 and discharged on day 7. Histamine levels in the vomited tuna slices sent from the emergency department were 109 mg/100 g, confirming the diagnosis of severe scombroid poisoning.

Help the clinician reach the correct diagnosis or management decision through structured deliberation.

2. **Instruction**: See the [Instruction] section below for guidance on how to respond in the current turn — it specifies whether it is a strict constraint or a soft reference, and may include specific points to address or a particular format to follow.
3. **Safety First**: Patient safety overrides politeness. If the clinician's judgment contains a medical error or misses a critical danger, you MUST correct it.
4. **Concise turns**: Each turn should be 2–4 sentences. Do not produce long lists or procedure walkthroughs.

[Case]
A woman in her 70s with rheumatoid arthritis who was receiving long-term immunosuppression (prednisolone and methotrexate) presented with a 6-month history of progressive papulonodules on her face and extremities. The patient, an avid gardener with regular soil exposure, reported no systemic symptoms, such as fever, cough, or weight loss. Initial laboratory investigations, including a complete blood cell count and biochemical tests, yielded unremarkable results. HIV screening results were negative, and chest computed tomography showed no evidence of pulmonary involvement. Physical examination revealed multiple papules and nodules, with seropurulent crusts on the face, dorsal hands, and extremities alongside rheumatoid joint deformities (Figure 1A). No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly was noted. Histopathological examination of lesional biopsy specimens from the face and hand showed identical features (Figure 1B).

[Instruction]
You MUST respond to the clinician based on the following behavioral instruction. This is a strict constraint — your response MUST conform to it, not merely consider it.

The clinician's latest claim has been validated as follows:
  Relation: supported
  Confidence: high

Initiating empiric clarithromycin (a macrolide) and ethambutol is a standard first-line regimen for atypical mycobacterial skin infections, especially while awaiting culture confirmation. Sending tissue for mycobacterial and fungal cultures is the definitive diagnostic step, and coordinating close follow-up is essential to monitor treatment response and manage drug interactions with methotrexate. The plan appropriately addresses both immediate antimicrobial coverage and long-term diagnostic precision.

Chest radiography (Figure 1) showed clear lung fields and pectus excavatum (PEX). The patient was referred for cardiology consultation, on which physical examination revealed normal jugular venous pressure without prominentxorydescent, normal cardiac auscultation, and marked depression of the sternum.

Three years ago, he developed involuntary shoulder shrugging and lip pursing. He denied dysphagia, dysarthria, ptosis, and diplopia and reported no relevant personal or family history. Prior glucocorticoid therapy for diagnosis of polymyositis had yielded no improvement. A 56-year-old woman with no history of rheumatic disease or hand injury presented to the rheumatology clinic with bilateral hand contractures. Fifteen months prior, she developed sudden onset of severe bilateral hand pain, swelling, and stiffness, which progressed to bilateral finger contractures over the next few weeks. Six months later, she underwent tenolysis and fasciectomy for her right (dominant) hand contracture, but it recurred within 6 months. Ibuprofen did not improve her hand pain, so she received prednisone (30 mg daily) and methotrexate (10 mg weekly), which partially relieved her pain but resulted in a 6.8-kg (15-lb) weight gain. Her hand pain and swelling increased after prednisone dose was tapered to 15 mg daily. Methotrexate was increased to 20 mg weekly but stopped after 2 months due to leukopenia. In the rheumatology clinic, physical examination revealed swelling and tenderness of bilateral wrists, metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, nodular palmar tendon thickening, and flexion contractures of all fingers (Figure 1). Results of tests for rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, and antibodies to cyclic citrullinated peptide, extractable nuclear antigens, and double-stranded DNA were negative. Hand radiographs showed mild interphalangeal joint spurring; ultrasound with color flow Doppler revealed hypervascularity and synovial thickening in several metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints but no joint effusions or tenosynovitis. Results of serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, cancer antigen 125 (CA-125), cancer antigen 19-9 (CA 19-9), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), pelvic ultrasound, chest/abdomen/pelvic computed tomography (CT), mammography, upper endoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal.

A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

[Management Options]
  A. Referral for mitral valve surgery
  B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
  C. Left bundle branch pacing
  D. β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

The patient has severe, rate-dependent functional mitral regurgitation that appears with left bundle branch block and resolves with normalization of conduction, indicating dyssynchrony-induced papillary muscle dysfunction is the primary mechanism. This is a classic indication for CRT to correct the electrical dyssynchrony and eliminate the mechanically induced MR, given her symptomatic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in the setting of CAD.

A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). He received intravenous ceftriaxone (2 g) and vancomycin (1 g) and 3 L of intravenous crystalloid, but hypotension persisted, so an infusion of norepinephrine was started. One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel). case_info.explanation: D. Prescribe intravenous diphenhydramine (25-50 mg) and famotidine (20 mg) for 5 days The key to the correct diagnosis is the recognition that rapid onset of diffuse erythematous rash, abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea, hypotension, and ECG changes after eating raw fish is consistent with scombroid poisoning. Administering clindamycin (choice A) is incorrect because toxic shock syndrome is unlikely without fever and elevated levels of inflammatory markers. Intravenous mannitol (choice B) is not recommended because the patient did not have neurologic symptoms of ciguatera fish poisoning (eg, paresthesia, cold allodynia). Hydrocortisone (choice C) is not indicated because adrenal crisis is unlikely without orthostatic hypotension, hyperpigmentation, and electrolyte disturbances. Approximately 3% of foodborne illnesses in the US annually are caused by ingestion of contaminated fish. Scombroid poisoning, also known as histamine fish poisoning, occurs when improperly stored fresh or frozen fish contain high levels of histamine.1,2Properly stored fish have tissue histamine levels less than 1 mg/100 g. Histamine levels greater than 50 mg/100 g can cause mild scombroid symptoms,1and levels greater than 100 mg/100 g cause severe symptoms.3In the US, between 2019 and 2025, 71 of 138 (51%) seafood-related toxicity reports to the Food and Drug Administration were attributed to histamine poisoning.4Scombroid poisoning occurs less commonly with ingestion of canned fish, Swiss and Gouda cheeses, and fermented products such as sauerkraut.5 ScombridaeandScomberosocidaefish species (tuna, mackerel, bonito, skipjack) contain large amounts of histidine in their muscles that can be converted into histamine by decarboxylase enzymes produced by gram-negative bacteria (eg,Escherichia coli, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa).6,7Nonscombroid species associated with histamine fish poisoning include amberjack, bluefish, mahi-mahi, sardine, yellowtail, and herring.8Fish with bacterial overgrowth, which typically occurs with storage at temperatures higher than 4 °C (39.2 °F), cannot be identified by appearance, texture, taste, or odor, and histamine is not destroyed by normal cooking temperatures.6 Scombroid poisoning typically presents with mild, self-limited symptoms of rash, flushing, headache, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, and palpitations1that develop within 10 to 90 minutes after ingestion.6Severe scombroid poisoning may cause angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm, respiratory distress, cardiac arrhythmia, myocardial infarction, and, rarely, death (<1%).1Most symptoms, regardless of their severity, resolve within 12 hours.8The differential diagnosis includes staphylococcal toxic shock syndrome, IgE-mediated fish allergy, and ciguatera poisoning. In a study of 19 patients with scombroid poisoning and cardiovascular complications, 14 of 15 (93%) with reported blood pressures had hypotension less than 90/60 mm Hg, and 4 patients required mechanical life support.9ECG findings with widespread ST-segment depression and ST-segment elevation in lead aVR were reported in 15 of 18 patients (83.3%). [Case Scenario]
A woman in her 40s with well-differentiated grade 3 neuroendocrine tumor of the pancreas with liver metastases undergoing treatment with oral cabozantinib presented to a routine oncology appointment with tongue lesions for 1 week. She reported mild tongue sensitivity, especially with spicy food, but denied pain or dysphagia. The dorsal and lateral tongue exhibited multiple well-demarcated, annular erythematous macules and patches with white borders (Figure). No other oral ulcers, gingival lesions, lymphadenopathy, or mucocutaneous findings were noted. She had been taking the same dose of cabozantinib (40 mg once daily) for 3 months prior. The only other medication was apixaban for venous thromboembolism, initiated 2 years prior. The cancer-directed treatment prior to cabozantinib was capecitabine/temozolomide (discontinued 4 months prior).

[Management Options]
  A. Pellagra
  B. Oral mucositis
  C. Oral candidiasis
  D. Geographic tongue

[Conversation]  (User = clinician, Medical = AI assistant)
User: This patient has classic geographic tongue, which is a benign inflammatory condition unrelated to her cabozantinib therapy. The lesions are asymptomatic except for mild sensitivity to spicy foods, and there is no evidence of stomatitis or mucosal ulceration typical of drug toxicity. Given the benign nature and her stable oncology regimen, the most appropriate next step is reassurance and conservative management, advising her to avoid spicy foods and monitor for any changes. I see no indication to alter her cabozantinib dose.
Medical: I agree completely. Geographic tongue is a benign, often idiopathic condition, and the appearance and symptoms you've described fit perfectly. Reassurance and avoidance of irritants like spicy foods is the standard of care, and there's no reason to suspect cabozantinib toxicity or alter her stable anticancer regimen.
User: Excellent, we are in full agreement on the diagnosis and management. I will document this as benign migratory glossitis, advise symptomatic care, and continue her cabozantinib as scheduled.
Medical: Perfect. That plan is sound and ensures we address her mild oral symptoms while maintaining her oncologic stability. Clear documentation will be helpful for future reference.
User: Our consensus is clear and the plan is straightforward. I'll proceed with reassurance and symptomatic management as agreed.
Medical: That's the right approach. Consistent follow-up will confirm the benign course and allow you to address any new concerns promptly.

[Management Options]

  C. Implant a cardioverter-defibrillator

The most appropriate next step is urgent coronary angiography and possible percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) to address the ischemic threat.

You are a cognitive-load rater for human–AI clinical collaboration. Given the clinician's
most recent statement and the AI assistant's reply to it, rate how much MENTAL EFFORT the
AI's reply demands of the clinician.

[What "cognitive burden" means here]
- It is the effort the clinician must spend to PROCESS and RESPOND to the AI's turn:
  re-examining their own reasoning, weighing new alternatives, defending a position,
  or producing a justification.
- Alignment/agreement is low burden (the clinician can accept passively).
- Opposition, and especially DEMANDS that the clinician reason or justify, are high burden
  (the clinician must actively re-derive or argue).

[CRITICAL — burden is independent of correctness]
- Rate ONLY the effort demanded, NOT whether the AI is medically right or wrong.
- A correct challenge and an incorrect challenge of EQUAL forcefulness impose EQUAL burden.
- Do not reward or penalize the AI for being right; you are not judging medical validity.

[Scale: integer 0–3]
- 0 = None:     AI agrees / affirms / confirms. No new reasoning is demanded.
- 1 = Low:      AI mostly agrees and adds a minor note or qualifier. The clinician may
                register it but is not required to re-reason.
- 2 = Moderate: AI surfaces an alternative, qualifies, or gently challenges the clinician's
                view. The clinician must weigh new information and reconsider.
- 3 = High:     AI opposes the clinician and/or demands they justify/defend their reasoning
                (e.g. "what rules out X?", "walk me through why..."). The clinician must
                actively re-derive or argue.

Output a single JSON object and nothing else.

[Case context]
A 60-year-old man presented with a 1-week history of progressive painless diplopia. He had a history of hypothyroidism and dyslipidemia, for which he took levothyroxine and rosuvastatin. He reported no changes in visual acuity or color vision; no ocular pain, erythema, or abnormal discharge; and no headaches, scalp tenderness, jaw claudication, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria, weakness, numbness, or ataxia. He did not have any constitutional or systemic symptoms. Physical examination showed an isolated limitation of right eye abduction. The remainder of the examination, including visual acuity, pupillary reaction, visual fields, and fundoscopy, was unremarkable. A magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the head showed abnormal thickening and T2 hyperintensity of the right lateral rectus muscle with T1-weighted gadolinium enhancement (Figure 1). Tests for infection and autoimmune disease had negative results.  Computed tomography of the abdomen and pelvis did not demonstrate any evidence of malignancy.

[Clinician's statement]
Agreed. Our plan is finalized: proceed with orbital biopsy and withhold steroids pending histology. I'll schedule the procedure.

[AI assistant's reply]
Perfect. This is the most evidence-based approach for this presentation. I'll await the biopsy results with you.

A woman in her mid-70s with a medical history of coronary artery disease (CAD) and left anterior descending artery stenting complained of unexplained dyspnea on exertion. An exercise transthoracic echocardiogram (TTE) was conducted by the referring cardiologist as part of the CAD follow-up, which resulted in an end-test uncontrollable cough with acute dyspnea. Coronary angiography was performed and showed no evidence of ischemic progression. Subsequent pulmonary evaluations, including respiratory functional assessments, walking tests, and thoracic computed tomography scans, yielded normal results. The patient was therefore referred to the university hospital. Upon arrival at the specialized cardiology consultation, the patient exhibited an anxious state associated with tachycardia and the same dyspnea. The initial TTE demonstrated severe mitral regurgitation (MR) with notable tenting and the absence of valve coaptation (Figure 1A). The left ventricular (LV) ejection fraction was preserved at 70%, without any wall-motion abnormality, no LV dilation, and preserved global longitudinal strain of −21%. The electrocardiogram (ECG) revealed a sinus tachycardia with left bundle branch block (LBBB). As the examination continued, the heart rate decreased, accompanied by the disappearance of the symptoms. TTE subsequently demonstrated regression of the MR, which became minimal, without any tenting (Figure 1B), while the ECG exhibited narrowing of the QRS complexes. These findings were confirmed by an exercise TTE, which rapidly showed recurrence of LBBB and severe MR, followed by acute dyspnea and multiple B lines at lung ultrasound.

[Management Options]
  A. Referral for mitral valve surgery
  B. Cardiac resynchronization therapy with biventricular pacing
  C. Left bundle branch pacing
  D. β-Blockers to prevent the onset of LBBB

The patient has severe, rate-dependent functional mitral regurgitation that appears with left bundle branch block and resolves with normalization of conduction, indicating dyssynchrony-induced papillary muscle dysfunction is the primary mechanism. This is a classic indication for CRT to correct the electrical dyssynchrony and eliminate the mechanically induced MR, given her symptomatic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction in the setting of CAD.
Medical: You've correctly identified that dyssynchrony from LBBB is driving the functional MR, and CRT is indeed the established treatment to address this mechanism. Given her symptomatic heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and rate-dependent symptoms, CRT would be the appropriate next step to improve synchrony and reduce regurgitation.
User: Agreed. Given the clear correlation between LBBB, tachycardia, and severe MR, and the resolution with normalized conduction, CRT is the definitive next step. I would proceed with a pre-implant workup, including coronary angiography review to confirm stent patency, and schedule for device placement.

Medical: Perfect. Confirming her coronary status via the recent angiogram and vascular access completes the essential pre-procedural checklist for a safe and effective CRT implantation. This targeted approach should resolve her rate-dependent functional MR and associated dyspnea.

[Case Scenario]
A previously healthy 65-year-old farmer presented to the emergency department with 5 hours of fatigue, nausea, lightheadedness, headache, chest pain, abdominal pain, and diarrhea that developed 1 hour after eating raw tuna sashimi. He took no medications, had no known allergies, and did not smoke or drink alcohol. On presentation, his blood pressure was 67/42 mm Hg; pulse, 87 beats/min; respiratory rate, 20 breaths/min; temperature, 36.9 °C (98.4 °F); and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. He was shivering, had an erythematous nonpruritic rash on his upper torso (Figure, left panel), and had diffuse abdominal tenderness, without rebound or guarding. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 14 300/µL (reference, 3900-9800/µL) with 78% (reference, 40%-70%) neutrophils and no eosinophils. Levels of hemoglobin, platelets, serum cardiac troponin T, and C-reactive protein were normal, as were erythrocyte sedimentation rate and results of basic metabolic panel, liver function tests, chest radiograph, and electrocardiogram (ECG). One hour later, he vomited and developed nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, ST-segment elevation in lead aVR, and ST-segment depressions in leads II, III, aVF, and V3-6 (Figure, right panel).
